question:
The following sentence has been divided into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
The meeting / will taking / place next / Wednesday.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. will taking.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "will taking" contains the grammatical error. The modal "will" must be followed by the base form (V1) of the verb, not the present participle (V-ing) form.

• Rule — Modal + Verb: A modal auxiliary (will, shall, can, could, may, might, must, should, would) is always followed by the first form of the verb (V1) without "to". The correct form here is "will take", not "will taking".

• Applying the rule: "The meeting will take place next Wednesday" is the grammatically correct sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "place next" is grammatically correct; it correctly follows "take" to form the phrase "take place next Wednesday".

• Option 3: "The meeting" is a correct noun subject and needs no correction.

• Option 4: "Wednesday." is a correct noun (day) used correctly as the object of "next".

NOTE

• Common modal + verb errors tested by SSC: "will taking" → "will take", "can went" → "can go", "must doing" → "must do".

• Remember: modals never take "-s", "-ing", or "-ed" endings on the verb that follows them.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
Urgent activities are those things / that you must do immediately, / as they require quick action / and cannot be put on.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. and cannot be put on.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "and cannot be put on" contains the error. The correct phrasal verb here is "put off", meaning to postpone or delay something, not "put on" (which means to wear or to switch on).

• Rule — Phrasal Verb usage: "Put off" = to postpone; "put on" = to wear/switch on; "put up with" = to tolerate. The context of "urgent activities...that cannot be delayed" requires "put off", not "put on".

• Corrected sentence: "Urgent activities are those things that you must do immediately, as they require quick action and cannot be put off."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "that you must do immediately" is grammatically correct as a relative clause modifying "things".

• Option 3: "Urgent activities are those things" is a correct subject-verb-complement structure.

• Option 4: "as they require quick action" is a correctly formed subordinate clause of reason.

NOTE

• Commonly confused phrasal verbs in SSC exams: put off (postpone), put on (wear), put up with (tolerate), put across (communicate clearly), put down (write down/suppress).

• "Cannot be put off" is a passive construction meaning "cannot be postponed".

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
(1) When Christy (2) grew out, (3) he turned out (4) to be a gentleman.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. 2 (the segment "grew out").

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in part (2) "grew out". The correct phrasal verb is "grew up", meaning to become an adult / to develop from childhood to maturity.

• Rule — Phrasal Verb usage: "Grow up" means to mature or become an adult; "grow out" is not an idiomatic phrase in this sense ("grow out of" exists, meaning to become too big/old for something, but requires "of" and a following object, which is absent here).

• Corrected sentence: "When Christy grew up, he turned out to be a gentleman."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (segment 4 — "to be a gentleman") is grammatically correct; it correctly completes "turned out to be".

• Option 2 (segment 3 — "he turned out") is grammatically correct; "turned out" correctly means "eventually became/proved to be".

• Option 4 (segment 1 — "When Christy") is a correct subordinate clause opener and needs no correction.

NOTE

• Commonly confused phrasal verbs: grow up (mature), grow out of (become too old/big for), grow into (develop into), grow apart (become distant).

• "Turn out" (to eventually prove to be) is a frequently tested phrasal verb in SSC error-spotting questions.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
Rashmi was / quite amusing when / she heard about / what had happened.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. quite amusing when.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "quite amusing when" contains the error. Since Rashmi is the person experiencing the feeling (not the one causing amusement in others), the past-participle adjective "amused" must be used instead of the present-participle adjective "amusing".

• Rule — "-ing" vs "-ed" adjectives: The "-ing" form (amusing, boring, interesting) describes the person/thing that causes the feeling; the "-ed" form (amused, bored, interested) describes the person who experiences the feeling.

• Corrected sentence: "Rashmi was quite amused when she heard about what had happened."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Rashmi was" is a correct subject + verb combination and needs no change.

• Option 3: "she heard about" is grammatically correct as a subordinate clause.

• Option 4: "what had happened" correctly uses the Past Perfect tense to show an action completed before another past action (she heard).

NOTE

• Other commonly tested "-ing/-ed" adjective pairs: boring/bored, interesting/interested, exciting/excited, confusing/confused, tiring/tired, surprising/surprised.

• Trick to remember: the person feels the "-ed" emotion; the thing/situation is "-ing".

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

There is nothing more (1)__________ than when you sit down at your table to study with the most sincere of intentions and instead of being able to finish the task at hand you find your thoughts (2)__________. However, there are certain techniques that you can use to (3)______ your concentration. To begin with, one should (4)______ to create the physical environment that is conducive to (5)_____ thought.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 1
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. frustrating.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "frustrating" fits the context best — the passage describes the annoying/exasperating experience of sitting down with sincere intentions to study but being unable to finish the task, which is a frustrating situation.

• Rule — Contextual vocabulary: The blank must logically connect to the rest of the sentence — "instead of being able to finish the task... you find your thoughts (wandering)" — this failure to concentrate despite good intentions is best described as "frustrating", not merely exciting or surprising.

• Complete sentence: "There is nothing more frustrating than when you sit down at your table to study with the most sincere of intentions and instead of being able to finish the task at hand you find your thoughts wandering."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "exciting" is incorrect — an inability to concentrate while studying is not an exciting experience.

• Option 3: "surprising" is incorrect — there is nothing unexpected about losing concentration; it does not fit the tone of mild exasperation.

• Option 4: "interesting" is incorrect — it has a positive connotation that contradicts the negative experience being described.

NOTE

• In cloze passages, always read the whole passage first to grasp the overall tone (here, a mildly negative/exasperated tone about difficulty concentrating) before choosing an option for each blank.

• Words like frustrating, irritating, exasperating, and annoying often appear together as near-synonyms in SSC vocabulary-based cloze questions.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

There is nothing more (1)__________ than when you sit down at your table to study with the most sincere of intentions and instead of being able to finish the task at hand you find your thoughts (2)__________. However, there are certain techniques that you can use to (3)______ your concentration. To begin with, one should (4)______ to create the physical environment that is conducive to (5)_____ thought.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. wandering.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "thoughts wandering" is a standard collocation meaning the mind drifting away from the task at hand and not staying focused.

• Rule — Collocation: Certain words habitually pair together in English (collocations). "Thoughts/mind + wander" is a fixed and natural collocation used to describe a lack of concentration, which fits the context of being unable to finish the study task.

• Complete sentence: "...instead of being able to finish the task at hand you find your thoughts wandering."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "worrying" is incorrect — "thoughts worrying" is not idiomatic; one's thoughts do not "worry", a person worries.

• Option 2: "tiring" is incorrect — "thoughts tiring" is not a natural collocation in English.

• Option 3: "interesting" is incorrect — it does not describe the drifting, unfocused nature of thoughts implied by the context.

NOTE

• "Wandering mind/thoughts" is a common phrase in passages about concentration and study techniques.

• Related expressions: "mind wanders off", "lose one's train of thought", "daydream".

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

There is nothing more (1)__________ than when you sit down at your table to study with the most sincere of intentions and instead of being able to finish the task at hand you find your thoughts (2)__________. However, there are certain techniques that you can use to (3)______ your concentration. To begin with, one should (4)______ to create the physical environment that is conducive to (5)_____ thought.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. enhance.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "enhance" means to improve or increase the quality/effectiveness of something, which fits perfectly with "techniques that you can use to enhance your concentration".

• Rule — Contextual vocabulary: The sentence discusses positive techniques to help with a problem (losing concentration), so a positive, improvement-related verb is needed. "Enhance your concentration" is a standard, natural collocation.

• Complete sentence: "However, there are certain techniques that you can use to enhance your concentration."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "convince" is incorrect — one cannot "convince" one's concentration; "convince" takes a person as its object, not an abstract quality like concentration.

• Option 3: "commit" is incorrect — "commit your concentration" is not idiomatic English.

• Option 4: "discover" is incorrect — the passage is about improving an existing ability (concentration), not finding something new.

NOTE

• "Enhance" commonly collocates with: enhance performance, enhance skills, enhance concentration, enhance productivity.

• Distinguish enhance (improve) from enforce (compel obedience) and ensure (make certain) — these are commonly confused in SSC vocabulary questions.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

There is nothing more (1)__________ than when you sit down at your table to study with the most sincere of intentions and instead of being able to finish the task at hand you find your thoughts (2)__________. However, there are certain techniques that you can use to (3)______ your concentration. To begin with, one should (4)______ to create the physical environment that is conducive to (5)_____ thought.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. attempt.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "attempt" means to try to do something, which fits the sense of "one should attempt to create the physical environment that is conducive to focussed thought" — i.e., one should try/make an effort to set up the right environment.

• Rule — Contextual vocabulary: "Should + attempt + to + verb" is a natural structure meaning "should try to". The sentence is giving practical advice, so a verb meaning "try/make an effort" fits.

• Complete sentence: "To begin with, one should attempt to create the physical environment that is conducive to focussed thought."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "announce" is incorrect — one does not "announce" to create an environment; "announce" means to make a public statement, which is out of context here.

• Option 3: "imagine" is incorrect — the passage recommends actual, practical action (creating a real environment), not merely imagining one.

• Option 4: "lead" is incorrect — "lead to create" is not idiomatic; "lead" does not fit grammatically or contextually with the infinitive "to create" here.

NOTE

• "Attempt to + verb" and "try to + verb" are interchangeable structures frequently tested in SSC cloze passages.

• Watch for words that are grammatically plausible but contextually wrong (like "announce" or "lead") — always check meaning-fit, not just grammatical fit.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

There is nothing more (1)__________ than when you sit down at your table to study with the most sincere of intentions and instead of being able to finish the task at hand you find your thoughts (2)__________. However, there are certain techniques that you can use to (3)______ your concentration. To begin with, one should (4)______ to create the physical environment that is conducive to (5)_____ thought.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 5
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. focussed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "focussed" (British spelling of "focused") means concentrated/attentive, which fits the phrase "conducive to focussed thought" — i.e., an environment that helps one think with concentration.

• Rule — Contextual vocabulary: The whole passage is about improving concentration; the physical environment being created should therefore be conducive to "focussed" (concentrated) thought, tying back to the passage's main theme.

• Complete sentence: "To begin with, one should attempt to create the physical environment that is conducive to focussed thought."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "dazzling" is incorrect — it means impressively bright or skillful, which does not fit the context of concentrated thinking.

• Option 3: "cautious" is incorrect — cautious thought relates to carefulness/wariness, not to the concentration theme of the passage.

• Option 4: "joyful" is incorrect — it relates to happiness, which is unrelated to the passage's theme of concentration.

NOTE

• "Focussed" (double s) is the British spelling; "focused" (single s) is the American spelling — both are acceptable, but SSC papers often use the British form.

• The whole passage revolves around the theme of concentration; when solving cloze passages, keep the central theme in mind while choosing each option.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
My sister’s paintings were ________ at the national museum.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. on display.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct preposition to use with "display" (in the sense of being shown/exhibited) is "on" — the fixed phrase is "on display", meaning exhibited or shown publicly.

• Rule — Fixed Prepositional Phrase: "On display" is an idiomatic prepositional phrase used specifically to describe items being exhibited (e.g., in a museum, shop, or exhibition). It does not take "in", "upon", or "into".

• Complete sentence: "My sister's paintings were on display at the national museum."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "in display" is incorrect — "in display" is not a standard English phrase.

• Option 3: "upon display" is incorrect — "upon" is not used with "display" in this idiomatic sense.

• Option 4: "into display" is incorrect — "into" implies movement into something, which does not fit the static sense of items being exhibited.

NOTE

• Other fixed preposition + noun phrases frequently tested by SSC: on sale, on show, on offer, on loan, in stock, on demand.

• "Display" as a noun almost always pairs with "on" (on display) in this exhibiting sense; as a verb, it takes a direct object without a preposition (e.g., "the museum displayed the paintings").

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Stick to one’s guns
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. To remain faithful to.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Stick to one's guns" means to firmly maintain one's position, opinion, or decision despite pressure or opposition to change it — that is, to remain firm and faithful to one's own stand. (अपने रुख पर अडिग रहना)
◦ Example: Despite criticism from his colleagues, he stuck to his guns and refused to change the report.

• The expression originates from a military context, where soldiers were expected to hold their firing position ("stick to their guns") rather than retreat, even under attack.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: To become a rebel (विद्रोही बनना): To openly resist or oppose authority — not the meaning of this idiom.

• Option 2: To shoot at (गोली चलाना): The literal, non-idiomatic meaning of "guns" alone; not the sense intended here.

• Option 3: To become unfaithful to (बेवफा होना): This is the opposite of the idiom's actual meaning.

NOTE

• Other idioms of firmness/determination often asked in SSC: "Hold one's ground", "Not budge an inch", and "Stand one's ground" (all meaning to refuse to change one's position).

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Litrature.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Literature" — written and spoken works, especially those considered of superior or lasting artistic merit. (साहित्य) The given word "Litrature" is missing the "e" after "Lit" and is therefore misspelt.

• Spelling key: LIT + ER + A + TURE. Note the sequence "liter" (as in "literal") followed by "ature". The word comes from the Latin litteratura, meaning "writing".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Reformation" is correctly spelt — the act of improving something by removing faults.

• Option 3: "Schedule" is correctly spelt — a plan for carrying out a process, giving the times at which events are intended to happen.

• Option 4: "Miserable" is correctly spelt — very unhappy or uncomfortable.

NOTE

• Commonly misspelt SSC words related to "Literature": literary, literate, literal — all retain the "liter-" root spelling.

• Always check for missing/extra vowels in the middle of long words — this is the most common type of spelling trap in SSC papers.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can replace the bracketed word segment in the following sentence.
An (imperfect positioning) of the Sun, Earth and Moon results in the Moon passing through only part of Earth’s umbra, resulting in a partial lunar eclipse.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. imperfect alignment.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "imperfect positioning" refers to the Sun, Earth and Moon not being in a perfectly straight line. The most precise substitute is "alignment", which means the arrangement of objects in a straight line or in a particular relative position.

• Rule — Contextual word substitution: When substituting a bracketed segment, the replacement must preserve the exact original meaning while using natural, idiomatic English. "Alignment" of celestial bodies is the standard astronomical term for their relative positioning, matching "positioning" precisely.

• Corrected sentence: "An imperfect alignment of the Sun, Earth and Moon results in the Moon passing through only part of Earth's umbra, resulting in a partial lunar eclipse."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "imperfect alliance" is incorrect — "alliance" means a partnership/union, unrelated to physical positioning.

• Option 2: "imperfect revolution" is incorrect — "revolution" refers to orbital motion around a body, not relative positioning.

• Option 3: "imperfect allegiance" is incorrect — "allegiance" means loyalty, which is meaningless in an astronomical context.

NOTE

• Commonly confused words: alignment (arrangement in a line), alliance (partnership), allegiance (loyalty), revolution (orbit/rotation) — all share similar sounds but very different meanings, a frequent SSC trap.

• In astronomy, "syzygy" is the technical term for a straight-line alignment of three celestial bodies (as in eclipses).

question:
Select the option that can substitute the bracketed word segment meaningfully.
The city of Hyderabad is located (on the heart from Telangana).
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. in the heart of Telangana.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiomatic phrase to describe a location in the central/most significant part of a region is "in the heart of" + place name. The correct preposition combination is "in the heart of Telangana".

• Rule — Fixed Prepositional Phrase: "In the heart of" is a standard fixed expression meaning "in the central part of". It always takes "in" before "heart" and "of" before the place name — no other preposition combination is grammatically acceptable.

• Corrected sentence: "The city of Hyderabad is located in the heart of Telangana."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "with the heart in Telangana" is incorrect — this is not an idiomatic or grammatically standard phrase.

• Option 2: "in the heart with Telangana" is incorrect — "with" cannot follow "heart" in this fixed phrase.

• Option 3: "of the heart in Telangana" is incorrect — the word order and prepositions are reversed and non-idiomatic.

NOTE

• Similar fixed locative phrases tested by SSC: "in the middle of", "at the centre of", "on the outskirts of", "in the vicinity of".

• "Heart of" (figurative, central part) should not be confused with "by heart" (memorised) or "heart-to-heart" (an intimate conversation).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
Anthony Trollope was an industrious and disciplined writer.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Lazy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "industrious" means hardworking, diligent, and devoted to one's work. Its most appropriate antonym among the given options is "Lazy", meaning unwilling to work or use energy; idle.

• Rule — Antonym selection: An antonym must be the direct opposite in the same part of speech and register as the original word. "Industrious" (hardworking) is directly opposed by "lazy" (unwilling to work), whereas the other options describe unrelated qualities.

• Illustrative opposite sense: "Anthony Trollope was a lazy and undisciplined writer" (opposite meaning).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Exhausting" is incorrect — it means causing extreme tiredness, which is not the opposite of "hardworking".

• Option 2: "Skittish" is incorrect — it means nervous or easily frightened (often used for horses/people), unrelated to industriousness.

• Option 3: "Dizzy" is incorrect — it means feeling unsteady/confused, unrelated to the concept of hard work.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "industrious": diligent, hardworking, assiduous, sedulous, hard-working.

• Other antonym pairs frequently tested: diligent × lazy/indolent, active × lethargic, sincere × careless.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the word ‘Contaminate’ from the given sentence.
She spent the entire night working non-stop to clean the blood stains from the rug.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. clean.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Contaminate" means to make something impure or dirty by adding a polluting substance. Its direct antonym is "clean", meaning to make free from dirt, marks, or mess.

• Rule — Antonym selection from context: The sentence "she spent the entire night working non-stop to clean the blood stains from the rug" already contains the word "clean" used as a verb, which is the precise opposite action of "contaminate" (to dirty/pollute).

• Illustrative opposite pair: to contaminate (make dirty) × to clean (make free from dirt).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "rug" is incorrect — it is simply a noun (the object being cleaned), not related in meaning to "contaminate".

• Option 2: "spent" is incorrect — it refers to the passing of time, unrelated to contamination.

• Option 3: "working" is incorrect — it refers to the act of labouring, not to purity/impurity.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "contaminate": pollute, taint, defile, adulterate, infect.

• Other antonym pairs: pollute × purify, taint × sanitise, infect × disinfect — frequently tested in SSC vocabulary-in-context questions.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Frivolity
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Insignificance.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Frivolity" means the quality of not being serious or sensible about something important; triviality or silliness. Among the given options, "Insignificance" (the state of being unimportant or trivial) is the closest match. (तुच्छता)
◦ Example: The judge criticised the frivolity of the lawsuit, as it had no significant legal merit.

• Rule — Synonym selection: A synonym should carry the closest overall sense of the original word. "Frivolity" and "insignificance" both relate to a lack of seriousness, weight, or importance, unlike the remaining options.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Consequence (परिणाम): Means a result or effect — the opposite sense of triviality.

• Option 2: Substantial (पर्याप्त/ठोस): Means large in amount or importance — an antonym-like sense, not a synonym.

• Option 3: Meaningful (सार्थक): Means having a serious, useful, or purposeful meaning — again close to the opposite of "frivolity".

NOTE

• Related words: frivolous (adjective, not serious), levity (light-heartedness in a serious context), triviality, silliness.

• Be careful in synonym questions where distractor options are actually antonyms in disguise (as with "substantial" and "meaningful" here).

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Have a bee in your bonnet
option_1: Be preoccupied or obsessed with something
option_2: Unable to stay at a place for long
option_4: Having a cruel intention or grudge against someone
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Be preoccupied or obsessed with something.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Have a bee in your bonnet" means to be preoccupied or obsessed with an idea, or to keep thinking and talking about something constantly. (किसी बात पर सनक सवार होना)
◦ Example: She has a bee in her bonnet about recycling and never stops talking about it.

• The expression evokes the image of a bee buzzing around trapped inside one's bonnet (hat), constantly causing agitation — much like an obsessive thought that will not leave one's mind.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Unable to stay at a place for long (एक जगह टिक न पाना): This describes restlessness, which is the meaning of a different idiom, "to have itchy feet" or "a rolling stone".

• Option 3: To keep worrying about yourself (स्वयं की चिंता करना): This describes self-concern, not obsession with an idea.

• Option 4: Having a cruel intention or grudge against someone (द्वेष रखना): This is closer to the idiom "to have a bone to pick with someone" or "to bear a grudge", not this one.

NOTE

• Other insect-related idioms tested by SSC: "Butterflies in one's stomach" (nervousness), "As busy as a bee" (very hardworking), "To make a beeline for" (to go directly/quickly towards).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
There is no way I can swallow the ghastly medicine.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. horrible.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "ghastly" means extremely unpleasant, horrible, or causing horror/fright. The most appropriate substitute among the options is "horrible", which carries the same negative, unpleasant connotation.

• Rule — Substitution of underlined word: The replacement must preserve both the meaning and the negative tone of the original sentence — "I can't swallow the ghastly medicine" implies the medicine tastes/feels terrible, which "horrible" conveys accurately.

• Corrected sentence: "There is no way I can swallow the horrible medicine."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "comforting" is incorrect — it means providing comfort/consolation, the opposite of the intended negative sense.

• Option 3: "agreeable" is incorrect — it means pleasant or acceptable, contrary to "ghastly".

• Option 4: "pleasant" is incorrect — it means enjoyable/agreeable, again the opposite of the intended meaning.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "ghastly": dreadful, horrid, gruesome, hideous, appalling.

• Antonyms of "ghastly": pleasant, agreeable, delightful, comforting — useful to remember since these often appear as distractor options in the same question.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word in the given sentence.
The recent cloudburst completely dismantled the village and its people.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. took apart.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "dismantled" means to take something apart/pull it down piece by piece, or to destroy its structure completely. The most appropriate substitute is "took apart", which conveys the same sense of complete structural destruction.

• Rule — Substitution of underlined word: The replacement phrase must retain the original sense of thorough physical destruction, matching the intensity implied by "completely dismantled".

• Corrected sentence: "The recent cloudburst completely took apart the village and its people."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "took back" is incorrect — it means to reclaim or retract something, unrelated to destruction.

• Option 3: "took after" is incorrect — it means to resemble (usually a family member), completely unrelated in meaning.

• Option 4: "took up" is incorrect — it means to begin an activity or occupy space/time, unrelated to destruction.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "dismantle": demolish, destroy, wreck, raze, break down.

• "Take apart" as a phrasal verb can also mean to criticise something severely (figurative use), in addition to its literal meaning of physically disassembling something.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
Please don’t touch that, it’s flammable .
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Non-combustible.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "flammable" means easily set on fire; capable of burning quickly. Its most direct antonym is "Non-combustible", meaning not capable of burning or catching fire.

• Rule — Antonym selection: The antonym must directly negate the core property described by the original word (capability of catching fire). "Non-combustible" is the precise technical opposite of "flammable", formed by negating "combustible" (capable of burning) with the prefix "non-".

• Illustrative opposite pair: "it's flammable" (catches fire easily) × "it's non-combustible" (cannot catch fire).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Nonexplosive" is incorrect — it means not liable to explode, which relates to explosion, not the general capacity to catch fire.

• Option 3: "Incendiary" is incorrect — it actually means capable of causing fire, which is close in meaning to "flammable" rather than its opposite.

• Option 4: "Fire-resistant" is incorrect — it means able to withstand fire without much damage, a related but less precise/direct opposite than "non-combustible".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "flammable": combustible, inflammable (note: "inflammable" is NOT an antonym of "flammable" despite the "in-" prefix — both mean the same thing, i.e., capable of burning).

• This is a classically tricky SSC vocabulary pair — remember "flammable" = "inflammable" (same meaning), while "non-flammable"/"non-combustible" are the true opposites.

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Immigrete.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Immigrate" — to come to live permanently in a foreign country. The given word "Immigrete" incorrectly ends in "-ete" instead of the correct "-ate", making it misspelt.

• Spelling key: IM + MIGR + ATE. The root "migr" (from Latin migrare, to move) is common to migrate, emigrate, and immigrate; the correct ending is always "-ate", not "-ete".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Combat" is correctly spelt — to fight or take action against something.

• Option 3: "Relevant" is correctly spelt — closely connected or appropriate to the matter at hand.

• Option 4: "Professional" is correctly spelt — relating to or belonging to a profession.

NOTE

• Related words that share the "migr" root and the "-ate" ending: migrate, emigrate, immigrate — all commonly confused for their prefixes (im-, e-) which indicate direction (into vs. out of a country).

• Always check word endings like "-ate" vs "-ete" vs "-it", as SSC frequently tests this type of ending confusion.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
The new chief is gifted at the power of eloquence.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. gifted with.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined segment "gifted at" is a preposition error. The correct and idiomatic collocation is "gifted with", used when referring to someone possessing a natural talent, quality, or ability.

• Rule — Fixed Preposition with "gifted": When "gifted" describes someone possessing a particular skill, quality, or ability, it is followed by the preposition "with" (e.g., "gifted with intelligence", "gifted with a beautiful voice"). "Gifted at" is used only when followed directly by a gerund/skill area (e.g., "gifted at painting"), but here it is followed by a noun phrase "the power of eloquence", which requires "with".

• Corrected sentence: "The new chief is gifted with the power of eloquence."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "gifted for" is incorrect — "gifted for" is not a standard idiomatic combination in English.

• Option 3: "gifted among" is incorrect — "among" implies being part of a group, which does not fit the sense of possessing a talent.

• Option 4: "gifted of" is incorrect — "of" is not used after "gifted" in this possessive-quality sense.

NOTE

• "Gifted with" + noun (a talent/quality) vs. "gifted at" + gerund (an activity): e.g., "gifted with intelligence" but "gifted at solving puzzles".

• Similar preposition pattern: "blessed with" (a quality), "endowed with" (a quality) — both function like "gifted with".

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Fastidious
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Lax.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Fastidious" means very attentive to and concerned about accuracy and detail; excessively particular or hard to please. Its direct antonym is "Lax", meaning not sufficiently careful, strict, or exact; careless.

• Rule — Antonym selection: An antonym must express the opposite degree of care/strictness. "Fastidious" (extremely careful/particular) is directly opposed by "lax" (careless/not strict), whereas the remaining options describe unrelated qualities such as timing or speed.

• Illustrative opposite pair: a fastidious editor (extremely careful about detail) × a lax editor (careless about detail).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Scrupulous" is incorrect — it is actually a synonym of "fastidious" (meaning careful and diligent), not an antonym.

• Option 3: "Late" is incorrect — it relates to timing, unrelated to the concept of care/particularity.

• Option 4: "Speedy" is incorrect — it relates to quickness, unrelated to the meaning of "fastidious".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "fastidious": meticulous, particular, scrupulous, finicky, pernickety.

• Antonyms of "fastidious": lax, careless, casual, easy-going, undemanding — SSC frequently places a synonym (like "scrupulous" here) as a distractor in antonym questions.

question:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence.
I was looking for a barren seat in the bus but could not find one.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. vacant seat.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined phrase "barren seat" uses the wrong adjective. "Barren" means infertile or unproductive (typically of land) and does not collocate with "seat". The correct word is "vacant", meaning empty or unoccupied, which is the standard collocation with "seat".

• Rule — Collocation/word choice improvement: The adjective chosen to modify a noun must be one that habitually and meaningfully pairs with it. "Vacant seat" (an empty, unoccupied seat) is the natural, idiomatic English collocation, whereas "barren" is reserved for land, soil, or (figuratively) a barren mind/period.

• Corrected sentence: "I was looking for a vacant seat in the bus but could not find one."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "hollow seat" is incorrect — "hollow" means having an empty space inside a solid object, not "unoccupied"; it does not fit the sense of an available seat.

• Option 2: "deserted seat" is incorrect — "deserted" is used for places left empty by people (e.g., a deserted street/village), not typically for a single seat.

• Option 4: "vacuous seat" is incorrect — "vacuous" means lacking thought or intelligence (e.g., a vacuous expression/remark), and is never used to describe a physical seat.

NOTE

• Commonly confused near-synonyms of "empty": vacant (unoccupied, e.g., a seat/post/house), barren (infertile, e.g., land), hollow (empty inside a solid object), vacuous (lacking thought/intelligence), deserted (abandoned by people, e.g., a place).

• "Vacant" is the standard SSC-tested word for an unoccupied seat, post, or room.
